1.3.1 Reading - K. Nandra (2007)  [1]

Covers 37 observations of 26 Seyfert galaxies from XMM-Newton

All show Iron K emission, which makes this paper useful for candidate selection for our research
Around 45% of the data was best fit with a relativistically blurred reflection model

Some objects may not show the broadening?


General background information

Iron line emission broadening predicted in Fabian et al (1989)
This was alongside the discovery that the emission likely comes from the accretion disk
Useful reads?

Fabian (1989)
George, Nandra & Fabian (1990)
Tanaka et al. (1995)


Data Reduction

They give a lot of detail on their data reduction which may be useful further down the line
Source taken from a circle with radius 700 detector pixels
There are several windowing modes on the CCD which will be important to note

Model

They found that the minimum set of models was:

Power law continuum (modelling the corona)
Reflection model (e.g. XILLVER)
Can use relativistic blurring on this however not necessarily needed
Ionized absorber model

The models used are covered in depth, including how they selected if and how to apply the absorber models

1.4 2026/09/26

1.4.1 Reading - Fabian et al. (2002)  [2]

1.4.1.1 Background

Presents preliminary results from a 325 ks observation of MCG-6-30-15

Data taken from both the EPIC MOS cameras and the EPIC pn camera in small window mode with a medium filter

Very clear detection of a strong, broad, and skewed iron line
Spectrum characterised well by a steep emissivity profile within 6\(r_g\) and a flatter profile beyond
Inner radius of emission appears to lie around 2\(r_g\)

This was measured from the fit, where the inner radius of the disc was a fitting parameter
The measurements are dependent on an assumed power-law continuum and lack of complex absorption above 2.5 keV

ASCA observation showed emission from an accretion disc extending from \(6-40r_g\) with an inclination of around \(30^\circ\)

Measured from Fe-k\(\alpha\) line

The red wing of the line extends below 4 keV which can be explained by the disc extending within 6 \(r_g\)

Why is this??
This implies rapidly spinning black hole (as ISCO shrinks with \(a_*\))




1.4.1.2 Fitting

Several models were used to fit the data, including a phenomenological model (parametersing the iron line with power law, Compton reflection, a narrow Gaussian at 6.4 keV and a broad Gaussian which was free)

This provided a good overall fit with \(\chi^2=984.1\) for 1034 degrees of freedom

How are the number of dof determined?

This was improved by allowing the narrow Gaussian to have some width, giving an “excellent” fit

Second model used the Laor (1991) emission line profile

Fits were insensitive to the outer radius of the disc, which was thus fixed at 400\(r_g\)
Free parameters were \(R_\text{in}\), the inclination, and the emissivity as a function of radius (parametrised as \(R^{-q}\))
Almost comparable \(\chi^2\) to the first model with two broad Gaussians

This falls short as with a simple power law emissivity, the red wing and narrow core of the line cannot be modelled simultaneously


Further improvements were made including

Addition of an iron K-edge

The K-edge is a sudden increase in x-ray absorption [FIND CITATION FOR THIS, wiki for now]
This significantly improved the fit
The K-edge however must be explained physically, several attempts were made

Neutral iron along the line of sight

This would require strong iron-L absorption, which is not present

Neutral iron outside the line of sight

Reflection off of distant material which would require strong reflection
This is inconsistent with the weak, narrow 6.4 keV iron line

Thick material partially covering the line of sight

This gave a comparable fit to the edge

Sako et al. (2002) suggested significant absorption due to inner-shell transitions of ionised iron

Explored using an absorption line model, giving a good fit

The complexity around 7.0 keV is emission

Recombination emission by H-like iron


It was not possible to determine whether the complexity was due to absorption or emission and both were thus considered

Use of a broken power law

This is not physically self-consistent

Ignores Fe K\(\beta\) at 7.05 keV
The high EW is not consistent with \(R_\text{refl}=1,\; i=30^\circ\), solar abundances and neutral
High abundance was investigated using 3\(\times\) the solar abundances which improved the fit significantly



Spectral variability was investigated by taking the ratio of the spectra resulting from two 10 ks intervals from the maximum and minimum flux periods

Taking the ratio of the two spectra showed clear signs
The iron line core is stronger in the low-flux spectrum

The models assume that the effects of ionized absorption are negligible above 2.5 keV, correct for absorption rising from low-Z elements, but may not be true if e.g. Si, S are present





[1] K. Nandra et al., Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society 382, 194 (2007).


[2] A. C. Fabian et al., (2002).

In order to avoid running all of the above commands upon every login session, the following was completed:

Data was downloaded using a wget command as follows:






TipData Download

This command can be reused for any observation ID by simply replacing the final part.

2.4.1.1 Pipeline Reprocessing
With this working, I began working through the XMM-SAS ABC guide for data reduction. Everything up to the end of the making a Light Curve section of the ABC guide is automated by the script provided by Darius Michienzi.
Run the script using
# Unzip any zipped files
gzip -d *.gz

# Run the script
julia /home/jq23394/XMM-data-reduction.jl
in the ODF directory. Set useful environment variables using:
export SAS_ODFPATH="$(pwd)"
export SAS_CCFPATH="/opt/local/XMM/ccf/"
export SAS_CCF="$SAS_ODFPATH/ccf.cif"
export SAS_ODF="$SAS_ODFPATH/$(ls *SUM.SAS)"
evselect table=mos1_filt.fits withrateset=Y rateset=mos1_ltcrv.fits maketimecolumn=Y timebinsize=100 makeratecolumn=yes


2.4.1.2 Time Filtering
The next step is to apply time filters, which can be done by looking at either the rate or the time intervals. To filter by rate, use the syntax
tabgtigen table=mos1_ltcrv.fits gtiset=gtiset.fits expression='RATE<=6' 
where the expression RATE<=6 selects all regions with a rate below 6 ct/s. To filter by time, use the syntax
tabgtigen table=mos1_ltcrv.fits gtiset=gtiset.fits timecolumn=TIME expression='TIME <= 73227600'
where the expression TIME<=73227600 selects the region below a given timestamp. Conditions can be combined using e.g. (EXP1)&&(EXP2)&&!(EXP3) which means that regions will be taken from expressions 1 and 2, and ignore anything that matches expresssion 3.
Either of these methods will generate a gti file, which can be used as
evselect table=mos1_filt.fits filtertype=expression filteredset=mos1_filt_time.fits expression='GTI(gtiset.fits,TIME)'


2.4.1.3 Image and Source Detection
After this, run
atthkgen atthkset=attitude.fits
Next, we produce images using binsizes of 22 or 82 for the MOS or PN cameras respectively. This corresponds to the size of the pixels of each on the sky, being 1.1” and 4.1”, respectively.
evselect table=mos1_filt_time.fits withimageset=yes imageset=mos1-s.fits imagebinning=binSize xcolumn=X ximagebinsize=22 ycolumn=Y yimagebinsize=22 filtertype=expression expression='(FLAG == 0)&&(PI in [300:2000])'

evselect table=mos1_filt_time.fits withimageset=yes imageset=mos1-h.fits imagebinning=binSize xcolumn=X ximagebinsize=22 ycolumn=Y yimagebinsize=22 filtertype=expression expression='(FLAG == 0)&&(PI in [2000:10000])'

evselect table=mos1_filt_time.fits withimageset=yes imageset=mos1-all.fits imagebinning=binSize xcolumn=X ximagebinsize=22 ycolumn=Y yimagebinsize=22 filtertype=expression expression='(FLAG == 0)&&(PI in [300:10000])'
replacing the options mos1_filt_time.fits and the image bin sizes as necessary.
Initial runs of this resulted in the error

Column `X' does not exist in table `/tmp/fileYpufn0:EVENTS'
Using ftlist on the filtered events file showed that the columns X and Y did not exist. Due to this the data used in the ABC guide was downloaded to test that the instructions work in the first place. It was noticed that during the reprocessing steps emproc and epproc, the messages

Due to the process getting stuck on the source detection edetect_chain step, it was decided to skip this step and manually select the source region, given it was easy to find in this data. The selection was done in ds9 via
ds9 mos1_filt_time.fits & 
The image, alongside the source and background regions, were selected as shown below



The regions used for spectrum extraction. The outer two circles were used to select an annulus for the background. The inner circle was used for the source region. The regions were centered at (25631.2,23903,300) with radii of 300, 500, and 1500 pixels.


An exposure map was made from the hard X-ray image via
# Generate Exposure Map
eexpmap imageset=mos1-h.fits attitudeset=attitude.fits eventset=mos1_filt_time.fits expimageset=mos1_expmap_2-10keV.fits pimin=2000 pimax=10000
The spectra could then be extracted as
# Extract the Source Spectrum
evselect table='mos1_filt_time.fits' energycolumn='PI' filteredset='mos1_filtered.fits' filtertype='expression' expression='((X,Y) in CIRCLE(25631.2,23903,300))' spectrumset='mos1_pi.fits' spectralbinsize=5 withspecranges=yes specchannelmin=0 specchannelmax=11999 

# Extract the Background Spectrum
evselect table=mos1_filt_time.fits energycolumn='PI' filteredset='bkg_filtered.fits' filtertype='expression' spectrumset='bkg_pi.fits' spectralbinsize=5 expression='((X,Y) in CIRCLE(25631.2,23903,1500))&&!((X,Y) in CIRCLE(25631.2,23903,500))' withspecranges=yes specchannelmin=0 specchannelmax=11999
The spectrum was checked for pileup with
# Check for Pileup
epatplot set=mos1_filtered.fits plotfile=mos1_epat.ps useplotfile=yes withbackgroundset=yes backgroundset=bkg_filtered.fits
which output the following graph



The output of epatplot. The modelled distributions agree well with the observed distributions (as seen in the lower panel) and therefore pileup can be neglected here.


# Find the source and background region areas for the ancillary file
backscale spectrumset=mos1_pi.fits badpixlocation=mos1_filt_time.fits
backscale spectrumset=bkg_pi.fits badpixlocation=mos1_filt_time.fits

# Generate the Photon Redistribution Matrix
rmfgen rmfset=mos1_rmf.fits spectrumset=mos1_pi.fits 

# Generate the Ancillary File
arfgen arfset=mos1_arf.fits spectrumset=mos1_pi.fits withrmfset=yes rmfset=mos1_rmf.fits withbadpixcorr=yes badpixlocation=mos1_filt_time.fits 
With these files successfully generated, it was possible to plot the spectrum through a quick Julia script, making use of the SpectralFitting.jl package
using SpectralFitting, Plots

function LoadData(
    spectrum::String, background::String, response::String, ancillary::String; 
    dataRange::Tuple{Real, Real}=(3,10)
    )

    data = OGIPDataset(
        spectrum; 
        background = background, 
        response = response, 
        ancillary = ancillary
    )

    # Regrouping, normalising, dropping bad channels and curtailing
    regroup!(data)
    normalize!(data)
    drop_bad_channels!(data)
    mask_energies!(data, dataRange...)
end

# Setting the instrument as a variable for generaliseability
instrument = "mos1"

data = LoadData(
    "$(instrument)_pi.fits",
    "bkg_pi.fits",
    "$(instrument)_rmf.fits",
    "$(instrument)_arf.fits"
)

plot(data)

6.2.1 Julia Plotting of XSPEC Output
XSPEC outputs data as a .qdp file which is similar in structure to a CSV other than a header with the structure:
READ SERR 1 2
@ratio_plot.pco
!
and different datasets are separated with a line
NO NO NO NO NO
where there is a “NO” for each column of data. The routine produced therefore runs as follows:

The file is read as a string
The header is removed by taking the part of the file following the !
The number of columns is counted by counting the number of spaces on a single line
The datasets are split using the separator shown above
Each dataset is converted into a dataframe which is stored in an array and returned

The source code is shown below
function ParseQDP(filename)

    # Open the file
    fileString = open(filename) do file
        read(file, String)
    end

    # Removing the header from the top of the file
    fileString = fileString[findfirst("!", fileString)[end]+2:end]

    # Getting the number of columns
    numcols = count(" ", fileString[1:findfirst("\n", fileString)[1]]) + 1

    # Splitting the datasets
    splitter = join([("NO "^numcols)[1:end-1], "\n"])
    strings = split(fileString, splitter)

    # Generating numbered header
    header = join([join(1:numcols, " "), "\n"])

    # Creating an empty array for each dataset
    output = Array{DataFrame}(undef, length(strings))

    # Assembling dataframes
    for (i, string) in enumerate(strings)
        output[i] = DataFrame(CSV.File(IOBuffer(join([header, String(string)]))))
    end

    return output
end

8.3.1 Further Automating Data Reduction
Given the large amount of data that needs reducing, it was decided to determine if it would be possible to further automate the data reduction. The three steps that need automation are:

Determining the good time interval
Selecting the source and background regions
Checking for pileup (and reducing the effects if pileup is present)

It was decided to first tackle the source detection, which can be split into two steps:

The centroid detection
Determining the size of the regions

To determine the centre, a python script was written making use of the astropy and photutils libraries. As the objects we are looking at are point sources, we can conveniently use a star finding algorithm. astropy was used to read in and manipulate the image, and the DAOStarFinder utility was used to detect the source. This works as our data currently consists of only a single source, however our procedure may need to be reconsidered if we use datasets where that is not the case. The current version of the code is currently as follows
import numpy as np

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.colors import LogNorm

from astropy.io import fits
from astropy.stats import sigma_clipped_stats
from photutils.detection import DAOStarFinder

def FindSource(hdu):
    """
    Find the centre of the brightest source in an image
    """

    # Taking the data and conversion factor between image and detector coords
    data = hdu.data
    factor = hdu.header["CDELT1L"]

    # Detecting sources
    mean, median, std = sigma_clipped_stats(data, sigma=3.0)
    daofind = DAOStarFinder(fwhm=3.0, threshold=1*std)
    sources = daofind(data - median)

    # Taking the brightest source detected
    source = sources[sources["mag"] == sources["mag"].min()]

    source = np.array([source["x_centroid"].data[0], source["y_centroid"].data[0]])

    return source, factor
This simply returns the centre coordinates (in image coordinates) and factor is the conversion factor between image and detector coordinates. The second step of the source region selection was produced by my partner, and these can be combined into the routine.
The pileup check is similarly trivial to automate, as we can simply assume no pileup for now and manually reprocess cases where pileup is a factor. This is currently assumed to be a valid approach as pileup does not seem to be an issue for our data, however if it becomes more prevalent in future investigations, this may need to be re-evaluated.
Automating the good time interval selection will be the next step, this may be possible through simply defining a threshold (for example within a given number of \(\sigma\)).
As each automated step will be susceptible to errors due to assumptions made, each of these steps will be written such that they produce an output which can be inspected by a human. For the source detection, this will be a plot of the regions selected, and for the GTI selection this will be a plot showing the threshold.

The next step to automate is the GTI filtering, which can be done by looking at the distribution of the light curves. By simply finding the mean count rate, we can filter for the data to be within a given number of standard deviations as follows
from astropy.io import fits
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

def FindBounds(data, sigma=1):

    mean = np.mean(data)
    std = np.std(data)

    expression = f"(RATE<={mean+std})&&(RATE>={mean-std})"

    return expression, mean, std

9.3.1 Automating Region Selection
The previous method of background region selection suffered from two main issues:

It a lot of the time included parts of the psf of the source
It included unused regions of the chip, which can skew the measurements

With this in mind, it was decided to pursue a different approach, taking the regions in the furthest corner of the chip. A geometrical approach was found as follows



An example source image with the regions we want to take. The green regions are background and the blue region is source. Several coordinates and lines are shown which will be the basis of the selection algorithm.


To select these regions, the following algorithm is proposed

Find the centre of the source using the previous DAOStarFinder implementation (\(P_s\))
Find the corners of the window within the image (\(P_1,P_2,P_3,P_4\))

This can be done by finding the first/last rows/columns of the image that contain data

Take the two corners furthest from the source and draw a line between them (\(\ell_{23}\))
Draw a line from the source which perpendicularly bisects the line found (\(\ell_s\)) in the previous step and find the intercept between the two (\(P_i\))
The radii of the background regions can be taken from the distances between this intercept and each respective corner (\(|\vec{P}_2-\vec{P}_i|\) and \(|\vec{P}_1-\vec{P}_i|\))

This will include some margin \(m_1\) to account for point spread and error \[r_{b,j} = \frac{1}{2}\left(\left|\vec{P}_j-\vec{P}_i\right| - m_1 - m_2\right)\]
where \(m_2\) is a margin from the frame of the window

The lines connecting opposing corners (\(\ell_{b,1}\) and \(\ell_{b,2}\)) can then be found, and the centres of the background regions can be found by moving a distance along this line equal to \[\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{2(d_{b,j} + m_2)^2}\]

where \(d_{b,j} = 2r_{b,j}\)
The \(+ m_2\) ensures that the region is a distance \(m_2\) from the border of the window

Finally, the radius of the source region can be determined as the perpendicular distance from the source to the line connecting the two closest corners (\(\ell_{41}\)) minus the margin \(m_2\)
